Without this branch that answer falls through to "the server answered" and is rendered as a result in the grey of a finished thing - so an operator who sent SaveWorld and got a receipt would read it as a save that landed, which is the exact belief that stopped a cluster into three worlds still being written

guards.disable: if False:  # GUARD DISABLED BY MUTATION CHECK
guards.why: a refused RCON connection has two opposite meanings - the world has closed, or the server has not opened its RCON port yet - and only the container tells them apart. Reading a refusal from a RUNNING container as "exited" is what let a stop signal three booting servers into a kill-revive-boot loop, so exited may only ever be true for a map whose container is gone

guards.disable: swap_files, why_build = bool(ready) and owns_updates(store), ""  # GUARD DISABLED BY MUTATION CHECK
guards.why: the disable text is the exact gate apply_batch used to carry, and it is too weak: `staging_mode: always` rehearses the build already RUNNING as routine bookkeeping, which writes a verified primed record for it, so `bool(ready)` reads that as work to do. Pressing Apply then stopped ten servers to install what they were already on - and a needless full restart IS an ARK apply, so it is a live route into the stop path. The comparison that makes the difference is newer_build(installed, staged), and it has to be asked HERE, inside the verb: the gate used to live at the callers, empty_watch and due() got one, and the manual apply was added later without one

guards.disable: if False:  # GUARD DISABLED BY MUTATION CHECK
guards.why: the third state again, on the panel whose docstring says it gets its own colour rather than quietly rendering as a tick. Two of the apply refusals are determinations - the staged build IS the one running, or IS older - and grey is right for a settled answer. The third is the absence of one: the install could not be read at all, which on Unraid is an unmounted share or the wrong Ark root. Without this branch it wore the same grey under a bold 'Apply is off', three lines below a version row reading 25117056 -> 25200000 update available, so an operator scanning the bold read 'you are current' about a question Obelisk never managed to ask. Matched on identity with updates.UNREADABLE and not on words in the sentence, because that text is refusal and log text too and a reword must not be able to drop the colour back to grey

guards.disable: first = SERVER_EXE if SERVER_EXE in line else ""  # GUARD DISABLED BY MUTATION CHECK
guards.why: `docker top` on a running map returns THREE lines carrying ArkAscendedServer.exe and only one is the server: the other two are the Proton launcher (`proton run ArkAscendedServer.exe`) and the Steam wrapper (`steam.exe ArkAscendedServer.exe`). Only the FIRST token may ever be judged, and the disable text is the containment test somebody will write instead - it reads either wrapper as a server, which holds a stop for ever waiting on a process that has already gone, and on the day it is inverted reads a wrapper's absence as the server being gone and signals into a save still being written. Observed at The Center on 2026-09-18

guards.disable: if False:  # GUARD DISABLED BY MUTATION CHECK
guards.why: PROCESS_GONE is the one state a stop may be signalled in, and it requires positive evidence of absence: a process listing that was read and had no server in it. A listing that failed, timed out or raised establishes nothing - and without this branch it falls straight through to PROCESS_GONE, which is a Docker hiccup deciding to stop a container whose server is still writing its save-on-exit. The same conservative reading _might_be_running already makes of an unanswerable Docker, one layer down

guards.disable: return first == SERVER_EXE  # GUARD DISABLED BY MUTATION CHECK
guards.why: the two directions of this test are not symmetric. Reading a wrapper as a server only HOLDS a stop - safe, and visible. Failing to recognise the REAL server reads a live map as PROCESS_GONE, which is the one state that authorises a signal, and on a first look close_map acts on it with no save and no DoExit in front - so a casing or quoting change in the launch line would stop a container whose world is live and unsaved. The disable text is the narrow compare this was written as first, and five real spellings fall through it: arkascendedserver.exe, ARKASCENDEDSERVER.EXE, ./ArkAscendedServer.exe, a quoted one, and Z:\ARK\ArkAscendedServer.exe

guards.disable: return (got.get(name) or {}).get("state") != "running"  # GUARD DISABLED BY MUTATION CHECK
guards.why: container_details skips any container whose `docker inspect` returned an error, so a Docker hiccup arrives as an empty answer that looks exactly like a container that is genuinely gone. The disable text is that reading, and it is the last fail-OPEN direction this mechanism had - close_map treats STOPPED as terminal success, so it would report a clean stop over a map whose server is still live and unsaved.
